title: Perplexity
subtitle: Topic: Perplexity · Subject: Natural Language Processing · Three beginner, two medium and two advanced questions, seven original educational diagrams and a tested next-token Python calculation.
hero:
PERPLEXITY · VISUAL STUDY

How well does a language model predict the next token?

Perplexity summarizes the probabilities assigned to observed text. Learn the formula, work through a calculation, compare evaluation protocols, and discover what the metric cannot tell you.

All probabilities in the diagrams are teaching examples; they are not measurements from a live LLM.

questions.stem: What is Perplexity in autoregressive Natural Language Processing, and what does it measure when a language model predicts the next token?
options: Perplexity averages the reciprocals of the probabilities for observed next tokens. It therefore gives each token's reciprocal probability equal weight before averaging, rather than combining their log probabilities.

Perplexity exponentiates the average confidence assigned across the full vocabulary at every position. It measures how certain the model feels overall, even when actual next-token probabilities are low.
Perplexity exponentiates the mean negative log probability of observed next tokens. Lower scores mean these tokens were more likely under the same held-out corpus, tokenization and scoring rules.

Perplexity measures the fraction of generated tokens that match a reference word for word. Lower values indicate fewer exact mismatches, regardless of the model's probabilities for alternative tokens.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Perplexity measures how much probability an autoregressive language model assigns to the next tokens that actually occur in held-out text. Compute the mean negative log probability and exponentiate it. A lower result means the model assigned greater likelihood under the same evaluation setup. For an autocomplete system seeing 'The kitten ...', assigning 50% probability to the observed word 'slept' gives that token less surprise than assigning 10%. This is a prediction-likelihood metric, not a percentage of correct words.
questions.figure:
QUESTION 01 · VISUAL LESSON

Perplexity uses probabilities for observed next tokens, not the fraction of exact next-token guesses.

questions.stem: How do you calculate Perplexity for three observed next tokens with probabilities 0.5, 0.25 and 0.125, and why do log probabilities help?
options: Take negative base-2 logs of the probabilities to get 1, 2 and 3 bits. Their mean is 2 bits, so perplexity is 2 raised to 2, or 4.
Take the reciprocal of each observed probability to obtain 2, 4 and 8, then average those numbers. This gives perplexity about 4.67 instead of averaging the negative log probabilities.

Multiply the three token probabilities to obtain 1/64, then invert this sequence probability directly. This gives perplexity 64 because each token receives its own contribution to total sequence likelihood.
Average the three observed probabilities to obtain about 0.292, then take its reciprocal. This gives perplexity about 3.43 by using the probability of a typical token instead of log probabilities.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The observed probabilities are ½, ¼ and ⅛. Their negative base-2 logs are 1, 2 and 3 bits, so average surprise is 2 bits per token. Exponentiating with base 2 gives perplexity 2² = 4. Natural logs give the same result when you use exp afterward. For a three-token weather bulletin, this summarizes the model's geometric-average likelihood of the actual words rather than merely averaging their probabilities.
questions.figure:
QUESTION 02 · VISUAL LESSON

Use matching log and exponential bases: PPL = 2^(mean bits) = exp(mean nats).

questions.stem: How is Perplexity related to average negative log-likelihood or cross-entropy loss, and how should two scores be interpreted on the same evaluation text?
options: Perplexity is the average negative log-likelihood itself, so a cross-entropy of ln 2 gives perplexity 0.69. Exponentiation would double-count the effect of language-model uncertainty.

Perplexity equals the square root of average negative log-likelihood, making rare-token errors less influential. Two models with equal average losses can still have different perplexities under the same log base.

Perplexity uses the sum of negative log-likelihood across a corpus without dividing by scored-token count. Longer evaluation documents therefore have intrinsically higher valid perplexity under otherwise identical conditions.
Perplexity exponentiates mean negative log-likelihood of observed next tokens. On the same scoring setup, losses ln 2 and ln 4 become perplexities 2 and 4.
questions.explanation: Explanation: For a causal language model, average negative log-likelihood (cross-entropy on observed next tokens) becomes perplexity when exponentiated. Thus mean losses ln 2 and ln 4 correspond to perplexities 2 and 4. Lower is better when both models score the same text with compatible tokenization and context rules. For two keyboard language models evaluated on the same chat messages, this comparison shows which assigned greater probability to the real next tokens. It does not establish which writes more helpful replies.
questions.figure:
QUESTION 03 · VISUAL LESSON

Perplexity = exp(mean negative log-likelihood). Always normalize by valid scored tokens.

questions.stem: Why is it misleading to compare Perplexity scores directly when language models use different tokenizers, datasets or evaluation protocols?
options: Perplexity becomes comparable as long as models process the same original characters, even if one tokenizer splits a word into many pieces. Both models then have identical prediction units and likelihood denominators.

Perplexity averages surprise per scored token; different tokenizers or test corpora change what is counted. Match evaluation protocols or use appropriate normalization before comparing scores for fair evaluation.

Perplexity depends mostly on model parameter count, while tokenization only changes how text is displayed. Holding model size constant is therefore sufficient to compare per-token scores between unrelated corpora.

Perplexity values can be compared directly after converting all logarithms to the same base. Tokenization, scored-token counts and context windows then cancel automatically from the resulting exponential average.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Perplexity averages surprise per token, but different tokenizers can split the same text differently. A toy tokenizer might keep 'unhappiness' as one unit while another uses three subword pieces. Both scores may be computed correctly yet measure different prediction units. Test corpus, context length, treatment of special tokens and other scoring rules also matter. For multilingual keyboards, always document the tokenizer and compare under matched evaluation settings; use more suitable normalized measures when tokenization differs.
questions.figure:
QUESTION 04 · VISUAL LESSON

Raw per-token perplexity is not necessarily comparable across different tokenizers.

questions.stem: How can a short Python script calculate Perplexity from true next-token probabilities while excluding padding and handling the next-token alignment correctly?
options: Take each actual next token's probability from its preceding context, exclude padding and ignored targets, then exponentiate mean negative log probability. Align tokens with the correct predictions.

Use each position's largest predicted vocabulary probability, including padding tokens, then exponentiate the negative log average. The most likely token gives a fair estimate even when the observed token differs.

Use the probabilities assigned to observed next tokens, but divide their total negative log-likelihood by all sequence positions including padding. Ignored tokens still belong in the denominator when they have probabilities.

Use the likelihoods of each token given both its previous and next tokens, then calculate the usual autoregressive perplexity. Conditioning on the actual future token does not alter the metric's interpretation.
questions.explanation: Explanation: A causal model predicts token i using only preceding tokens. Record the probability given to each actual next token, not the most probable alternative. Exclude padding and ignored positions from both the loss sum and token count, then compute exp(mean negative log probability). The Python example scores 'the', 'cat' and 'sat' with probabilities ½, ¼ and ⅛, skips padding and obtains perplexity 4.0. For real Transformers models, verify how labels are shifted internally to avoid off-by-one scoring errors.
questions.figure:
QUESTION 05 · VISUAL LESSON
Python · Standard library · 13 runnable lines (illustrative teacher-forced token probabilities)
from math import exp, log
tokens = ['the', 'cat', 'sat', '<PAD>']
prefixes = ['<BOS>', 'the', 'cat', 'sat']
true_token_probs = [0.5, 0.25, 0.125, 1.0]
valid_targets = [True, True, True, False]
losses = [-log(p) for p, keep in zip(true_token_probs, valid_targets) if keep]
if not losses:
    raise ValueError('No valid next-token targets')
mean_nll = sum(losses) / len(losses)
perplexity = exp(mean_nll)
print('Scored next tokens:', sum(valid_targets))
print('Mean negative log likelihood:', round(mean_nll, 4))
print('Perplexity:', round(perplexity, 2))

This self-contained code uses illustrative conditional probabilities; it does not call or download a language model.

questions.stem: What important limitations does Perplexity have when evaluating factual correctness, helpfulness, reasoning and the quality of generated language?
options: Low perplexity guarantees the model's generated answers are more faithful to retrieved sources, provided the test corpus is large enough. Human evaluation is mainly required when the tokenizer cannot represent rare words.

Low perplexity captures fluent language and correct reasoning simultaneously because both increase next-token probabilities. It is therefore a direct replacement for factuality checks if evaluation text resembles production prompts.

Perplexity measures likelihood of held-out tokens, not whether generated answers are factual, safe or useful. Evaluate those qualities separately using task outcomes, reference checks or carefully validated human assessments.

Perplexity reports how often a model's generated sentences contradict their own earlier statements. It therefore measures consistency and safety directly, while next-token prediction error requires a separate benchmark.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Perplexity reflects how well a model predicts tokens in evaluation text. It is useful for language-model likelihood, but it does not directly measure truth, instruction-following, reasoning, safety or helpfulness. A model could assign high likelihood to familiar yet misleading medical claims. Conversely, a model giving a precise but unusual answer might have higher perplexity on a particular corpus. For a question-answering assistant, assess factual support and task success separately rather than treating the lowest perplexity as automatically best.
questions.figure:
QUESTION 06 · VISUAL LESSON

Lower PPL on held-out text does not guarantee reliable factual answers or better generated responses.

questions.stem: How should Perplexity be evaluated responsibly on long documents and changing domains, including context-window limits, overlapping strides, uncertainty and fair benchmarking?
options: Split long documents into independent equal-sized chunks, always score every token in each chunk, and assume context boundaries have no effect. Repeatedly scoring overlap makes perplexity a more reliable average.

Evaluate on the model's training corpus and treat low perplexity as evidence of robustness to new subject areas. Reporting tokenization is unnecessary if the training loss used an exponential function.

Use sliding windows over long text but count overlapping context tokens in every loss average. Repeated context scoring is useful because it assigns extra weight to positions where the model has more history.
Score held-out text using valid preceding context and count each target once, even with overlapping windows. Document tokenizer, stride, context, domain slices and uncertainty for fair reports.
questions.explanation: Explanation: For a model with limited context, independently scoring disjoint chunks can deprive boundary tokens of useful history. Sliding or strided overlapping windows preserve more context, but tokens used only as overlap must not be counted repeatedly. Compare models on appropriate held-out corpora with documented tokenization, context, stride and valid-token counts. Inspect domain slices and uncertainty rather than reporting only one average. In a legal-document language model, low perplexity on contracts might not transfer to scientific articles or current legislation.
questions.figure:
QUESTION 07 · VISUAL LESSON

Overlapping context may be reused, but every scored target token should contribute only once.
